incident_summary: The log appears to show 2 degradation episodes, the first starting at 14:04:42 UTC, with 8 findings across 7 services. The likely causes, by severity, are: postgres-primary restart at 14:29:23 UTC (F5, critical); postgres-primary pool saturation at 14:05:02 UTC (F3, high). The episodes may be linked (H3). Recovery after E2 was observed, but the observation window is short.

primary.statement: The pool saturation in postgres-primary appears to be a probable origin of the degradation in E1, with downstream effects possible in api-gateway.
supporting: Strongest deviations in postgres-primary: active_connections 100 at max_connections=100, waiting_clients up to 31 vs baseline 0.
active_connections rose 30 → 100 while txn_per_s fell 107 → 51: connections appear to be held rather than serving load.
Later deviations in api-gateway follow: F4 (24 timeout, from 14:05:11), after the deviation in postgres-primary began at 14:05:02.
contradicting: Dependent services show deviations earlier: F1 at 14:04:42, F2 at 14:04:54, before postgres-primary at 14:05:02.

primary.statement: The restart in postgres-primary appears to be a probable origin of the degradation in E2, with downstream effects possible in api-gateway, billing-worker, inventory-service, notification-service, order-service and payment-service.
supporting: F5 records 7 restart events in postgres-primary from 14:29:23.

Later deviations in api-gateway, billing-worker, inventory-service, notification-service, order-service and payment-service follow: F6 (16 connection error, from 14:29:26), F7 (5 connection error, from 14:29:28), F8 (3 connection error, from 14:29:30), after the deviation in postgres-primary began at 14:29:23.

alternatives.statement: The degradation in E2 may be a consequence of E1, because postgres-primary did not return to its baseline in between.
supporting: Between E1 and E2 the source stayed off baseline: active_connections 53–61 vs baseline 30, idle_connections 22–29 vs baseline 48.
E2 starts at 14:29:23, 1103 s after E1 ended at 14:11:00.

alternatives.statement: The connection pool exhaustion in order-service and payment-service might be a client-side problem rather than a consequence of postgres-primary in E1.
supporting: F1 records 51 pool saturation events in order-service and payment-service from 14:04:42, with wait_ms up to 3000.
The deviation in order-service and payment-service began at 14:04:42, before postgres-primary at 14:05:02.
contradicting: Pressure on the database server is suggested by F3: 26 pool saturation at postgres-primary since 14:05:02.

alternatives.statement: A surge of incoming load at api-gateway might have contributed to the degradation in E1.
contradicting: Requests at api-gateway arrive at 1.3 per minute during E1 against 4.3 per minute in the baseline window (x0.31): a load spike is not supported by the log.

alternatives.statement: Unusual events in postgres-primary shortly before the onset of E1 might have triggered the degradation.
supporting: Events not seen in the rest of the baseline occur within 60s before the onset at 14:04:42: 3 x "checkpointer checkpoint_complete" in postgres-primary (14:04:31 to 14:04:40).

uncertainty.statement: The logs do not name the cause explicitly; the hypotheses are inferred from timing and dependencies and may be wrong.
The logs do not include query plans or statement statistics, so which queries became slow cannot be determined.
The logs contain no query-level records, so what held the client pool connections (long transactions, locks or slow queries) cannot be determined.
The logs contain no query-level records, so what held the database connections (long transactions, locks or slow queries) cannot be determined.
The logs do not show whether connection failures came from the network path, the database itself or client-side timeouts.
The logs do not show which transactions were aborted when connections dropped or whether their work was retried.
The logs show that the database process was killed but not who sent the signal (the OOM killer or an operator).
The logs do not include traffic metrics upstream of the entry point, so whether incoming load changed cannot be fully determined.
Recovery of E2 is observed, but the observation window after it is short.

severity_scale.criteria: User-facing requests fail (5xx/timeouts at an entry point) or a data store is unavailable (crash, restart, connections refused).
Errors inside a service or exhausted shared resources (connection pool, DB connections) that cause failed or aborted operations.
Degradation without outright failure: latency well above baseline, retries that eventually succeed, growing queues/backlogs.
Isolated warnings or minor deviations with no visible effect on requests.
